LONDON, England (CNN) -- A portrait painted 400 years ago and kept anonymously in an Irish home for much of the time since is now believed to be the only painting of William Shakespeare created during his lifetime. The portrait of William Shakespeare is thought to be the "only" portrait painted during his lifetime. The image reveals a wealthy Shakespeare of high social status, contradicting the popular view of a struggling playwright of humble status, according to Stanley Wells, a professor who chairs London's Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. Wells, a distinguished Shakespeare scholar, arranged for three years of research and scientific testing which confirmed it was painted around 1610, when Shakespeare would have been 46 years old. "A rather young looking 46, it has to be said," Wells said. Shakespeare died in 1616. The Cobbe portrait -- named after the Irish family that owns the painting -- shows Shakespeare with rosy cheeks, a full head of hair, and a reddish brown beard. The most common portrait of Shakespeare is a gray image showing a bald Bard with a small mustache and beard, and bags under his eyes. The identity of the man in the portrait was lost over the centuries -- until Alec Cobbe saw a portrait from Washington's Folger Shakespeare Library. That painting, which fell into disfavor as a Shakespeare portrait about 70 years ago, turned out to be one of four copies of Cobbe's portrait. The portrait "shows a man wearing expensive costuming, including a very beautifully painted ruff of Italian lacework which would have been very expensive," Wells said. "It establishes, for me, that Shakespeare in his later years was a rather wealthy, a rather well affluent member of aristocratic circles in the society of his time," Wells said. "There's been too much of a tendency to believe that Shakespeare, being the son of a glover, coming for a small town in the middle of England, that he necessarily retained a rather humble status throughout his life." Wells reads even more into what he sees in Shakespeare's newly-found face. "I think it's plausible as a portrait as a good listener, of somebody who would have been capable of writing the plays, clearly the face of a man of high intelligence," he said. "It's the face of a man, I think, who betrays a good deal of wisdom in his features. But, of course, as somebody (King Duncan) says in Shakespeare's story Macbeth, 'there's no art to find the mind's construction in the face.'" It should be noted that Shakespeare's King Duncan paid a price for judging Macbeth to have the face of an honorable man. Macbeth later murdered the king. The public can read Shakespeare's face from the original painting at Shakespeare Birthplace Trust in Stratford-upon-Avon where it goes on display for several months starting April 23. The portrait then returns to the Cobbe family, which inherited it when an ancestor married England's Earl of Southampton -- a friend of Shakespeare who likely commissioned its painting.

**HAS THE TRUE FACE OF SHAKESPEARE BEEN FOUND? EXPERTS UNVEIL RARE LIFETIME PORTRAIT**

**LONDON — March 9, 2009** — For nearly four centuries, the true appearance of William Shakespeare has been one of literature’s most enduring mysteries. Today, scholars and art historians announced what may be the breakthrough of the century: the identification of a portrait believed to be the only surviving likeness of the Bard painted during his lifetime.

The artwork, known as the "Cobbe portrait," depicts a handsome, stylishly dressed man with dark hair, a trimmed beard, and a faint, knowing smile. Unveiled today by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, the painting transforms the popular image of the world’s most famous playwright—replacing the familiar image of a solemn, balding man with that of a prosperous and attractive Elizabethan gentleman.

"The evidence that this is a portrait of William Shakespeare painted from life is overwhelming," said Professor Stanley Wells, chairman of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, during a press conference in London. "This is a momentous discovery for anyone who cares about Shakespeare, giving us a personal connection to a man who usually hides behind his texts."

### A Decades-Old Secret in a Country House

The portrait takes its name from the Cobbe family, who have held the painting in their private collection for roughly 300 years. For generations, it hung quietly in their ancestral home, Hatchlands Park in Surrey, misidentified as a portrait of the courtier Sir Walter Raleigh. 

The breakthrough occurred in 2006 when Alec Cobbe, an art restorer and family heir, attended an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery. There, he saw a famous painting known as the "Janssen portrait," which claimed to depict Shakespeare. Cobbe immediately recognized that the painting on display was an inferior copy of the artwork hanging in his own home.

Recognizing the potential significance of his family's heirloom, Cobbe brought the painting to the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, sparking a three-year forensic and historical investigation.

### The Scientific and Historical Evidence

To verify the portrait’s authenticity, an international team of experts subjected the painting to rigorous scientific testing. 

Tree-ring analysis (dendrochronology) confirmed that the wooden oak panel on which the portrait is painted dates to around 1610—a time when Shakespeare was at the height of his fame and wealth in London, around six years before his death. X-ray imaging and infrared reflectography further confirmed that the work was an original, created in a single sitting, rather than a later copy.

Crucially, researchers traced the provenance of the painting back to Henry Wriothesley, the 3rd Earl of Southampton. Wriothesley was Shakespeare’s primary patron and the man to whom the poet dedicated his romantic narrative poems *Venus and Adonis* and *The Rape of Lucrece*. Scholars believe Shakespeare may have commissioned the portrait specifically for his wealthy supporter.

Furthermore, technology revealed that at least five early copies of the Cobbe portrait were created during the 17th century, indicating that the original subject was a figure of immense public stature.

### A Striking New Likeness

Until now, the world’s understanding of Shakespeare’s appearance relied almost entirely on two posthumous images: the stiff copper-plate engraving by Martin Droeshout on the cover of the First Folio (1623), and the stark marble monument at Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon. Both were created years after his death by artists who likely never saw him.

The man in the Cobbe portrait—dressed in a costly silk doublet with a finely detailed lace collar—presents a stark contrast.

"It changes our whole impression of him," Professor Wells noted. "He doesn't look like a dry, dusty intellectual. He looks like a dashing, successful man of the world."

### Debate and Controversy

Despite the enthusiasm of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, the discovery has sparked lively debate among art historians. Several prominent experts have expressed skepticism, warning that identifying sitters from the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras is notoriously difficult.

Dr. Tarnya Cooper, curator at the National Portrait Gallery, suggested that while the painting is undeniably a high-quality 17th-century work, the subject could potentially be another prominent figure of the era, such as the poet Sir Thomas Overbury. 

"We welcome the research, but attributing unidentified portraits from this period requires extraordinary caution," Cooper said in a statement, noting that the gallery plans to continue studying the claim.

### Going on Public View

Regardless of the ongoing debate, the discovery has ignited massive interest worldwide. 

The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust announced that the Cobbe portrait will go on public display for the first time on April 23—traditionally celebrated as Shakespeare's birthday—at Hall’s Croft, an Elizabethan mansion in Stratford-upon-Avon that once belonged to Shakespeare’s daughter, Susanna.

For Alec Cobbe, the revelation is the culmination of a personal journey that has forever altered his family's legacy. 

"I always felt there was something extraordinarily compelling about this picture," Cobbe said. "To know that this might be the face that looked up from the manuscript of *Hamlet* or *The Tempest* is simply thrilling."

"This is not a portrait of a starving poet in a garret," said Sir Stanley Wells, honorary president of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and the world’s foremost Shakespeare scholar, who led the research. "This is a man of substance, a man of wealth, style, and high social standing. It shows someone who had made it to the very top of his profession and wasn't afraid to display his success."

The painting's journey to the public eye reads like a historical detective story. For nearly three centuries, the artwork hung quietly in an estate in Ireland, passed down through generations of the Cobbe family. For decades, the family believed the painting depicted Sir Walter Raleigh.

It was only after a family member visited an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery in London—and spotted a copy of the painting labeled as a potential portrait of Shakespeare—that the Cobbe family sought expert help.

Using tree-ring dating (dendrochronology) on the wooden panel, experts confirmed the wood originated from the same tree used by artists in London around 1610. X-ray analysis and pigment tests further proved that the portrait had not been painted over and was created during Shakespeare’s lifetime.

Crucially, digital imaging experts compared the Cobbe portrait to the famous Droeshout engraving—the iconic image of Shakespeare seen on the 1623 First Folio. The facial structures matched almost perfectly, leading Wells to conclude that the engraver of the First Folio likely used the Cobbe portrait as his primary source material after Shakespeare’s death.

"I am 90% convinced that this is William Shakespeare," Wells said. "To see the face of the creator of *Hamlet*, *Macbeth*, and *King Lear* as he actually looked while he was writing his late masterpieces is a deeply thrilling, game-changing moment in literary history."

**THE IRISH TIMES / INTERNATIONAL HERALD**

**‘The Holy Grail of Art History’: 400-Year-Old Painting Found in Irish Cottage Confirmed as Only Lifetime Portrait of Shakespeare**

**By Eleanor Vance**
*Art & Cultural Heritage Correspondent*

**DUBLIN —** For more than three centuries, it hung in a dimly lit hallway of a seaside cottage in County Kerry, overlooked as a portrait of a long-forgotten ancestor. 

Today, international art experts confirmed that the dusty, smoke-stained 17th-century oil painting is the ultimate literary treasure: the only surviving portrait of William Shakespeare painted while the playwright was still alive.

The discovery, described by art historians as "a once-in-a-century miracle," promises to solve one of the most enduring mysteries of English literature—what the Bard of Avon actually looked like.

The painting was uncovered last March by Moira Higgins, 42, while clearing out her late granduncle’s home near the town of Dingle. Intending to sell the house’s contents at a local auction, Higgins invited a regional appraiser to look over several older items. 

"I almost threw it out," Higgins said at a press conference at Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday. "It was covered in soot from the open fire, and the frame was rotting. We always just called him 'the brooding uncle.' To think I’ve been eating breakfast under the gaze of William Shakespeare my entire life is surreal."

### **A Scientific Breakthrough**

The artwork, painted on an oak panel, depicts a man in his late 40s with sharp hazel eyes, a receding hairline, a trimmed auburn beard, and a slight, enigmatic smile. He wears a dark velvet doublet and a simple, unadorned white linen collar—a departure from the elaborate lace ruffs typically seen in high-status Elizabethan portraiture.

Over the past nine months, the painting underwent rigorous, secret testing by an international team of conservators, dendrochronologists, and art experts at the National Gallery in London and the Hamilton Kerr Institute in Cambridge.

The results, released today, are conclusive:

* **Tree-ring analysis (Dendrochronology):** The oak panel was harvested from a tree in the West Midlands of England between 1604 and 1610.
* **Pigment analysis:** X-ray fluorescence revealed pigments unique to the early Jacobean era, including lapis lazuli and lead-tin yellow, with no modern synthetic compounds.
* **Infrared Reflectography:** Scans revealed underlying artist sketches showing adjustments made to the jawline and brow—proving the subject sat live for the painter, rather than being painted from memory or after death.

Most significantly, faint, microscopic lettering near the top left corner of the panel reads: *“Ætatis suæ 46”* (Aged 46) alongside the date *1610*—the exact year Shakespeare turned 46 while living in London.

"Until today, every known image of Shakespeare—including the famous Droeshout engraving on the First Folio and the Chandos portrait—was either created after his death or heavily disputed," said Dr. Alistair Finch, a senior fellow of the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. "This is it. This is the Holy Grail. For the first time, we are looking directly into the eyes of the man who wrote *Hamlet* and *King Lear* as he looked in the prime of his life."

### **How Did It End Up in Ireland?**

The provenance of the painting is still being pieced together, but researchers believe it arrived in Ireland during the mid-17th century. 

Archival research suggests the portrait was painted by Robert Peake the Elder, an Official Court Painter to King James I. Experts theorize the painting was commissioned by Henry Wriothesley, the 3rd Earl of Southampton—Shakespeare’s famous patron and rumoured close friend. 

During the turmoil of the English Civil War in the 1640s, a branch of the Wriothesley family fled to Munster, bringing a collection of personal effects with them. The portrait appears to have passed through generations of Irish landowning families before being purchased at a estate sale in the 1920s by Higgins’s great-grandfather, an avid collector of oddities.

### **Priceless Cultural Artifact**

While art market analysts hesitate to place a firm monetary value on a unique cultural artifact, preliminary estimates suggest the painting could be worth in excess of £100 million ($127 million USD) if placed on the open market.

However, Higgins has stated she has no intention of selling it to a private collector.

"He doesn't belong in a billionaire's basement," Higgins said. "He belongs to the world."

Higgins has agreed to a long-term loan agreement. The portrait will go on public display for the first time at the National Gallery of Ireland in Dublin this coming spring, before embarking on a global tour that will include stops in London, Stratford-upon-Avon, New York, and Tokyo. 

As for the face itself?

"He looks human," Dr. Finch remarked, gazing at the newly restored panel. "Not a grand god of poetry, but a tired, brilliant, thoughtful man who has seen the world and understands human nature better than anyone who ever lived."
